title: The 7 Types of Databases
eyebrow: Data systems · Match the database to the questions your software must answer
summary: Learn seven practical database families by starting with familiar data questions—orders, nested content, sessions, relationships, measurements, text search, and similarity—then continue into schemas, transactions, indexes, consistency, specialized stores, and production trade-offs.
prerequisites: How the Web Works helps show where a database sits behind a server, but this guide explains the data concepts it needs.
APIs and Data Exchange is helpful for understanding how other software asks a data-backed service for information, but it is not required to understand the database families.
learningOutcomes: Recognize relational, document, key-value, graph, time-series, search, and vector database families from the questions they are designed to answer well.
Choose a strong starting database by identifying what must be stored, which reads and writes matter most, what must stay consistent, and what operating constraints exist.
Explain when a specialized secondary store is justified and what synchronization, recovery, security, and operational costs appear when a system uses more than one database.

heroVisual.title: Seven families answer seven different question shapes
heroVisual.caption: This is a practical selection model, not a law that every product fits only one box. Many database products support features from more than one family.

nodes.label: Relational
nodes.detail: Which records are related, and can several connected changes remain correct together?

nodes.label: Document
nodes.detail: Can this nested record usually be stored and loaded as one meaningful unit?

nodes.label: Key–value
nodes.detail: I already know the exact key—what value belongs to it?

nodes.label: Graph
nodes.detail: How are these entities connected, and what paths link them?

nodes.label: Time-series
nodes.detail: How did this measurement change across time?

nodes.label: Search
nodes.detail: Which records best match these words and filters?

nodes.label: Vector
nodes.detail: Which stored items are mathematically most similar to this query or item?

sections.title: 1. Start with the questions your software must answer
sections.summary: A database is not chosen because its product name is popular. Start with the information you must preserve and the operations that must be fast and correct.

blocks.text: Imagine an online learning service. It stores users, subscriptions, courses, lessons, login sessions, search text, page-view measurements, and recommendation data. Those facts do not all create the same kind of question. 'Which invoices belong to this customer?' is different from 'give me session abc123,' 'find courses containing these words,' or 'which lessons are semantically similar to this question?' Database families exist because different data structures and workloads reward different storage and indexing strategies.

columns: Question the software needs to answer
rows: Which customer owns this order, and can payment + inventory updates obey shared rules?
Relationships, constraints, joins, and transactions are central.
Load this course with its nested lesson configuration as one unit.
The data naturally groups into a nested aggregate often read together.
I know session:8f21; return its value immediately.
The application already has the exact lookup key.
Which people are connected through this account, device, or transaction chain?
Variable-depth relationships and paths are the question.
How did CPU usage change minute by minute for the last 30 days?
Measurements are organized and aggregated around time.
Which articles match these words, filters, spelling variations, and relevance rules?
Text analysis and relevance ranking are the dominant retrieval needs.
Which documents are closest in meaning to this user question?
Retrieval depends on similarity between numeric vector representations.
blocks.caption: The question shape gives you a starting hypothesis, not a final purchase decision

blocks.text: Developers often call a recurring way the application reads or writes data an access pattern. Before choosing a database, write down the important access patterns in ordinary language: what must be saved, what must be looked up, what gets changed together, how much data exists, and how quickly the result is needed. Then add the correctness rules: which states must never occur, which operations must succeed or fail as one unit, and how much temporary inconsistency the product can tolerate.

items.title: List the facts that must survive
items.explanation: Name the durable information without choosing a database shape yet: users, orders, balances, content, events, measurements, relationships, and so on.
items.result: The data model begins from business reality rather than storage syntax.

items.title: Write the important reads as questions
items.explanation: Examples: 'load one order by id,' 'show invoices by customer and month,' or 'rank matching articles.' Include the latency the user or system actually needs.
items.result: The dominant access patterns become visible.

items.title: Write the important changes
items.explanation: Record how often data changes, which records change together, whether concurrent writers can conflict, and what must happen if part of a write fails.
items.result: Correctness and concurrency pressure become concrete.

items.title: State the rules that must never be violated
items.explanation: A rule such as 'an invoice number must be unique' or 'inventory cannot become negative after a completed sale' is an invariant: a condition the system must preserve as data changes.
items.result: Storage choices can be evaluated against actual guarantees instead of vague claims about consistency.

items.title: Add operating constraints
items.explanation: Include data volume, growth, backup/restore targets, availability, geographic needs, security/compliance, team skill, hosting limits, latency, and total cost.
items.result: The choice reflects the whole system rather than query syntax alone.

blocks.title: NoSQL is not one database type
blocks.body: The label NoSQL groups products with very different models and trade-offs. A document store, key–value store, graph database, search engine, and vector store should not be treated as interchangeable merely because they are not traditional relational systems.

blocks.prompt: You know a product supports millions of writes per second. Is that enough information to know it fits your billing system?
blocks.explanation: Throughput is only one constraint. You still need to know the billing data relationships, transaction and correctness rules, query patterns, failure behavior, recovery requirements, operational cost, and whether the team can run it safely.

sections.title: 2. Relational databases are strong when facts relate and rules span records
sections.summary: Rows live in tables, keys identify and connect records, constraints reject invalid states, SQL combines and transforms data, and transactions coordinate related changes.

visual.title: A relational model gives the database explicit rules
visual.caption: The database can enforce structure and relationships rather than relying on every application path to remember them independently.

nodes.label: Tables and rows
nodes.detail: Tables represent relations; rows contain individual records.

nodes.label: Columns and types
nodes.detail: Columns define named attributes and their permitted data types.

nodes.label: Keys
nodes.detail: Primary or unique keys identify records; foreign keys can enforce references between tables.

nodes.label: Constraints
nodes.detail: Rules such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and referential constraints reject invalid states.

nodes.label: Transactions
nodes.detail: A group of operations follows defined atomicity/isolation/durability behavior so related changes can be coordinated safely.

blocks.text: A relational database stores data in tables and relates records through values and keys. SQL, Structured Query Language, can select, filter, join, aggregate, insert, update, and delete data. A join combines related rows based on a relationship condition. The important advantage is not simply that SQL exists: the database can centrally enforce constraints and transaction rules that protect shared data across many application code paths.

blocks.code:
SELECT customer.name, SUM(invoice.total) AS lifetime_value
FROM customer
JOIN invoice ON invoice.customer_id = customer.id
GROUP BY customer.id, customer.name
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC;
blocks.explanation: FROM starts with customer rows. JOIN connects each invoice whose customer_id matches the customer's id. SUM adds invoice totals per customer. GROUP BY tells the database which rows belong in each aggregate result, and ORDER BY sorts customers by the calculated lifetime_value.

items.title: Strong starting fit
items.summary: Business data has important relationships, correctness rules span records, and future query combinations are not fully known in advance.
items.whenToUse: Orders, billing, inventory, permissions, scheduling, clinical/financial records, and many general application systems.

items.title: Index
items.summary: An additional data structure that helps the database find selected rows without scanning everything, at the cost of extra storage and write/update work.
items.whenToUse: Create indexes from measured query needs and execution plans rather than indexing every column by habit.

items.title: Transaction
items.summary: A unit of work whose changes follow the database's transaction guarantees, including whether all changes commit or roll back together and how concurrent work is isolated.
items.whenToUse: When several related reads/writes form one correctness boundary.
items.example: Record payment and update invoice state

blocks.title: A relational database is often a responsible default
blocks.body: For many business applications, relational constraints, transactions, mature tooling, flexible queries, and operational knowledge provide a strong baseline. Move to or add a specialized store when a measured workload or capability need justifies the additional model and operating cost.

sections.title: 3. Document databases keep data that belongs together in one nested record
sections.summary: A document model works naturally when an application usually creates, retrieves, and changes a nested unit together and its fields can vary between records.

blocks.text: A document database stores records as documents with named fields and nested structures, commonly in a JSON-like representation. The useful mental model is not 'schema-free.' It is 'the record boundary is often a nested aggregate instead of normalized rows spread across many tables.' An aggregate here means a group of related data the application treats as one consistency or loading boundary, such as a course plus its small ordered lesson configuration.

blocks.explanation: The course and its ordered lesson summaries are nested in one document, so an application that normally needs them together can retrieve one aggregate. Whether lesson content itself belongs here depends on growth, update patterns, sharing, and document-size/atomicity constraints.

items.title: Good fit
items.summary: Most reads and writes center on one naturally nested aggregate, optional fields vary, and cross-record relational rules are not the dominant challenge.
items.whenToUse: Content, catalogs, profiles, configuration aggregates, event-like payloads.

items.title: Watch the boundary
items.summary: Embedding everything can make documents grow without bound, duplicate shared information, or make independent updates contend on one large record.
items.avoidWhen: Many independently changing entities need rich joins or strict cross-record rules.
items.example: Do not copy a mutable customer profile into every order merely to avoid a relationship.

blocks.title: Flexible documents still have a schema
blocks.body: Applications depend on field names, types, required/optional values, indexes, validation, and migration behavior even when every document is not forced into identical columns. The schema may be more flexible or enforced in different layers, but it still exists as a contract.

blocks.prompt: A product record has a small list of display options that is always loaded and edited with the product. Does nesting those options automatically make the design wrong because it is not normalized into another table?
blocks.explanation: The right boundary follows ownership, read/write patterns, size, duplication, and consistency needs. A document model intentionally favors useful aggregate boundaries. Normalization is a powerful relational design technique, not a rule that every piece of nested data must be separated in every database family.

sections.title: 4. Key–value databases optimize the shortest path to a known item
sections.summary: When the application already knows the exact key, a key–value store can provide extremely direct reads and simple atomic operations without needing a general query language for every lookup.

visual.title: Known key versus open-ended question
visual.caption: This distinction explains both the strength and the limit of a key–value model.

nodes.label: Known key
nodes.detail: session:8f21 → retrieve the associated value. This is the natural key–value question.

nodes.label: Open-ended query
nodes.detail: Find every session for users in Louisiana created last month. That needs indexes/query structures beyond a plain direct-key model.

blocks.text: A key–value database maps a unique key to a value. Basic operations often look conceptually like get(key), set(key, value), delete(key), increment(key), or set an expiration. Some products such as Redis expose richer data structures and commands, but direct addressing by key remains a core mental model.

rows: A small boolean or configuration value.
blocks.caption: The key design is part of the data model because the application must know how to address the value

blocks.title: A cache participates in correctness
blocks.body: Once behavior depends on cached data, define expiration, invalidation, stale-data policy, stampede protection, eviction, persistence where relevant, and what the application does when the cache is unavailable. 'It is only a cache' does not remove these failure modes.

items.title: Good fit
items.summary: The dominant operation is direct lookup or a small atomic mutation by a known key.
items.whenToUse: Sessions, caching, counters, rate limits, ephemeral coordination, queue-like patterns supported by the chosen product.

items.title: Poor primary fit
items.summary: Users need rich ad hoc filtering, many joins, broad reporting, or questions whose lookup keys were not known in advance.
items.whenToUse: Keep a query-oriented authoritative store and use key–value as a focused companion where measured.

sections.title: 5. Graph databases make relationships part of the primary model
sections.summary: When the question repeatedly follows connections of changing depth, modeling nodes and relationships directly can make the data and queries match the problem more naturally.

visual.title: A recommendation question is a path question
visual.caption: Graph stores treat entities and the relationships between them as first-class parts of the model.

nodes.label: Person
nodes.detail: A node representing an entity with properties.

nodes.label: BOUGHT
nodes.detail: A typed relationship connecting the person to a product.

nodes.label: Product
nodes.detail: Another node in the graph.

nodes.label: SIMILAR_TO
nodes.detail: A relationship connecting products according to the domain model.

nodes.label: Candidate recommendation
nodes.detail: A result discovered by following a relationship pattern.

blocks.text: A graph database represents entities as nodes and connections as relationships or edges, usually with properties on one or both. A traversal follows those relationships. Graph databases become especially useful when relationship patterns and variable-depth paths are the recurring question—for example fraud rings, identity resolution, network topology, dependency chains, authorization relationships, and recommendation paths.

items.title: Good fit
items.summary: Queries repeatedly ask who/what is connected, through which relationships, and across an unpredictable number of hops.
items.whenToUse: Fraud/identity graphs, social relationships, network topology, dependency graphs, recommendation relationships.

items.title: Do not confuse capability with dominant workload
items.summary: Relational databases can store graph-shaped data and perform recursive/path queries too. The decision changes when graph traversal is frequent and important enough that graph-native modeling/query behavior materially reduces complexity or improves the needed workload.
items.avoidWhen: The data is mostly independent transactional rows with straightforward filters and aggregates.
items.example: A standard order ledger rarely needs a graph database solely because customers and orders are related.

sections.title: 6. Time-series, search, and vector stores optimize three specialized retrieval problems
sections.summary: These families often complement an authoritative business database because their indexing and storage structures are designed around measurements, relevance-ranked text, or similarity rather than general transactions.

items.title: Time-series database
items.summary: Stores measurements associated with time and optimizes time-window filtering, aggregation, retention, and downsampling. Downsampling replaces very detailed older samples with coarser summaries when that matches retention needs.
items.whenToUse: Infrastructure metrics, sensors, observability signals, market ticks, industrial measurements.
items.avoidWhen: Do not model every mutable business entity as a time measurement merely because records have timestamps.

items.title: Search engine
items.summary: Analyzes text and fields into structures such as an inverted index, which maps terms toward the documents containing them, then applies filtering and relevance scoring to return useful matches.
items.whenToUse: Site search, logs, product discovery, text-heavy filtering and ranking.
items.avoidWhen: Do not make a search index the only authoritative transaction store simply because search queries are fast.

items.title: Vector database or vector index
items.summary: Stores numeric vectors and retrieves nearby vectors using a distance or similarity measure, often with approximate-nearest-neighbor indexes for scale.
items.whenToUse: Semantic retrieval, recommendation candidates, image/audio/text similarity, retrieval for AI systems.
items.avoidWhen: Similarity cannot enforce exact business rules, permissions, factual truth, or identity equality on its own.

blocks.text: An embedding is a numeric vector produced by a model to represent features of an item such as text or an image. A similarity search compares those vectors and returns nearby items according to a mathematical distance/similarity rule. This can be useful for semantic retrieval, but the database is not 'understanding meaning' like a person. The embedding model, source data, distance metric, index configuration, metadata filters, and evaluation set all affect whether retrieved items are actually useful.

rows: How did this measurement change over a time window?
Asset/user/service metadata in a relational or document store.
Which records match this text + filters, ranked usefully?
Which stored items are closest to this vector under the chosen similarity model?
Source documents, permissions, and metadata in an authoritative store.
blocks.caption: Specialized indexes are often projections of data whose source of truth lives elsewhere

blocks.prompt: A vector search returns the nearest document to a question. Does 'nearest vector' prove the document is factually correct and safe to show?
blocks.explanation: Vector similarity is a retrieval signal, not a truth or authorization guarantee. Evaluate relevance, freshness, permissions, source quality, and downstream use separately.

sections.title: 7. Add another database only when its benefit pays for another source of failure
sections.summary: Using specialized stores together is often called polyglot persistence. It can solve real workload problems, but every extra copy introduces ownership, synchronization, security, recovery, and operating questions.

visual.title: One authoritative write can feed specialized read models
visual.caption: A projection is a derived copy shaped for a particular read/search/analysis need. The synchronization path becomes part of the system's correctness contract.

nodes.label: Authoritative write
nodes.detail: One system owns the accepted business change.

nodes.label: Change propagation
nodes.detail: Synchronous code, events, change-data capture, or another mechanism carries selected changes.

nodes.label: Projection
nodes.detail: A secondary model keeps only the fields/structure needed for a specialized read.

nodes.label: Specialized query
nodes.detail: Search, vector, time-series, cache, or graph workload reads its optimized representation.

nodes.label: Reconciliation
nodes.detail: Monitoring, retries, replay/rebuild, and audits detect or repair missing, duplicate, stale, or corrupt projections.

blocks.text: Polyglot persistence means intentionally using more than one data-storage technology because different parts of the workload benefit from different models. A common pattern is an authoritative relational store plus a search index or cache. The second store is not free performance: the system now has to decide who owns writes, how updates propagate, how stale the projection may be, what happens when propagation fails, and how deleted or security-sensitive data is removed everywhere it was copied.

items.title: Name the measured pressure
items.explanation: Show which query, latency, scale, text-relevance, graph, similarity, or time-series requirement the current design cannot meet acceptably.
items.result: The second store has a specific job instead of being architecture fashion.

items.title: Keep write ownership explicit
items.explanation: Choose where authoritative changes are accepted and which copies are derived projections.
items.result: Conflicting sources of truth are less likely.

items.title: Define propagation and freshness
items.explanation: State whether the projection updates inside the original request or later, and how much lag the product can tolerate.
items.result: Eventual consistency becomes a measurable product behavior rather than a vague disclaimer.

items.title: Make retries and rebuilds safe
items.explanation: The projection path should handle duplicate or missing deliveries, support replay/rebuild where appropriate, and avoid multiplying the authoritative effect.
items.result: A secondary store can recover after partial failure.

items.title: Observe drift and degraded behavior
items.explanation: Measure lag, failed updates, mismatched records, stale results, and what the application does if the specialized store is unavailable.
items.result: Silent inconsistency becomes visible and operable.

blocks.prompt: Search is slow, so you add a search engine populated from the primary database. Which store should normally decide whether an order payment actually exists?
blocks.answer: The explicitly designated authoritative store, not the derived search index.
blocks.explanation: The search engine can provide a fast searchable projection, but transactional truth and write ownership should remain unambiguous. If two stores can independently decide the same business fact, synchronization and conflict handling become much harder.

blocks.title: Simplicity has operational value
blocks.body: One well-modeled primary database with the right indexes is easier to secure, back up, restore, observe, migrate, and reason about than several stores. Add specialization after evidence shows its value exceeds that permanent operating cost.

sections.title: 8. Turn the seven families into a repeatable selection process
sections.summary: The family is a starting hypothesis. Validate it with representative data, the hardest reads and writes, failure tests, recovery tests, and realistic operating cost before committing to production architecture.

rows: Transactions, connected business records, constraints, evolving queries
Data model, transaction isolation, constraints, indexes/query plans, backup/restore, scale path.
Nested aggregate commonly retrieved and changed together
Aggregate boundary, document growth, duplication, validation, indexes, cross-document operations.
Direct known-key lookup, expiry, counters, cache/session behavior
Eviction, persistence, memory/cost, atomic commands, key design, outage behavior.
Modeling clarity, traversal latency, write/update patterns, indexes/constraints, operations.
Write rate, retention, downsampling, tag/cardinality model, query windows, compression/recovery.
Analyzers/tokenization, ranking evaluation, refresh lag, index size, rebuild/recovery, source-of-truth relationship.
Embedding model, distance metric, approximate-index recall/latency, metadata filtering, evaluation set, refresh/rebuild strategy.
blocks.caption: Use the workload to choose what to test—not a technology category to skip testing

items.title: Prototype the hardest questions
items.explanation: Use realistic record counts, value distributions, relationship depth, text, vector dimensions, and concurrent writes rather than toy data that makes every database look fast.
items.result: The prototype exercises the reason you are considering the technology.

items.title: Measure tail latency and resource cost
items.explanation: Average latency can hide bad slow cases. Measure percentiles such as p95/p99 where relevant and observe CPU, memory, storage, I/O, network, and hosted-service cost.
items.result: Performance is evaluated as a distribution with a price, not one benchmark number.

items.title: Test failure and recovery
items.explanation: Practice backup and restore, node/service interruption, bad deployment/data migration, and degraded dependencies—not only happy-path queries.
items.result: Recovery capability becomes evidence rather than documentation hope.

items.title: Evaluate security and operations
items.explanation: Review authentication, authorization, encryption, auditing, secrets, data deletion, upgrade/migration process, monitoring, support, and team expertise.
items.result: The database is judged as a production system the team must own.

items.title: Record the decision and rejected alternatives
items.explanation: State the workload, constraints, evidence, selected option, and conditions that would cause the decision to be revisited.
items.result: Future engineers can understand why the architecture exists instead of inheriting folklore.

glossary.definition: A recurring way an application reads or writes data, such as lookup by id, join by relationship, time-window aggregation, text ranking, or vector similarity search.
A condition the system must preserve as data changes, such as uniqueness or a business rule that forbids an invalid state.
A rule enforced by the database to reject data states that violate the declared model.
An additional data structure designed to speed selected retrieval patterns at the cost of storage and work when data changes.
A unit of database work whose operations follow defined commit/rollback, isolation, and durability guarantees.
A group of related data treated as one meaningful loading or consistency boundary in a domain model.
Following graph relationships from one node to connected nodes, potentially across several hops.
A search data structure that maps analyzed terms toward the documents or fields containing them so text matching can be efficient.
A numeric vector produced by a model to represent features of an item such as text or an image for downstream comparison or retrieval.
A derived representation of authoritative data shaped for a particular read, search, similarity, analysis, or caching need.
An architecture that intentionally uses multiple data-storage technologies because different workloads benefit from different models.
